summary.oneLineBrief: Little Rituals: the science behind why your grandmother was right, made into products you can trust.
neverDo: Make a parent feel guilty or inadequate
Use tradition as aesthetic without substance
Claim benefits without specific formulation evidence
Position against Indian traditional practices — the brand builds on them

primaryColor.rationale: The brand sits at the intersection of Indian tradition and modern formulation. The palette should feel warm, earthy, and considered — not the clinical white of pharma, not the aggressive green of greenwashing brands.

permitted: real hands holding real babies — not stock imagery
the oil catch the light — texture and warmth visible
the massage gesture — hands, touch, connection
Indian home contexts — natural light, warm settings
product alongside the practice, not instead of it
multigenerational if possible — grandmother and parent together
forbidden: Western lifestyle staging with baby as accessory
clinical white backgrounds with product only
fear-based imagery — rashes, distress, clinical close-ups of problem skin
overly produced perfection — real parents, real moments
photographyStyle.lightingMood: Warm afternoon light. The kitchen. The bedroom. The moment before the bath.

typographicVoice.sentenceStructure: Warm and conversational. Short to medium sentences. Never clinical lists as primary communication. "We spent six months getting this right" not "Formulated with key ingredients."
typographicVoice.punctuationStyle: Natural. Em dashes for warmth and parenthetical thought. No exclamation marks except in genuinely celebratory contexts. Never clinical.
typographicVoice.numeralStyle: Words for small numbers in prose. Numerals for specific formulation data. "Six months of testing" not "6 months". "0.1% fragrance" when specificity matters.

denotative.categoryDescriptor: Premium baby and child skincare — wood cold-pressed organic oils, science-formulated skin and hair care, made for Indian babies and Indian parents
functionalClaims: Wood cold-pressed at ambient temperature — no heat applied, nutritional profile preserved
Organic certification on oil range — [certification body to be specified]
Postbiotic formulation in face cream — supports baby skin microbiome barrier
Plant protein in shampoo and conditioner — nourishes without sulphates
Mineral sunscreen — physical UV block, no chemical UV filters
No parabens, no sulphates, no artificial fragrance in core range
specifications: Wood pressing preserves tocopherols (Vitamin E) and essential fatty acids that heat-pressing degrades
Baby skin is 20–30% thinner than adult skin — formulation absorbs and affects differently
Indian climate (humidity, UV index) creates specific skincare requirements not addressed by Western baby brands
forbiddenClaims: toxic-free — implies competitor products are toxic (legally and ethically problematic)
clinically proven to [outcome] — use specific study data or remove claim
best baby skincare in India — unprovable superlative
paediatrician recommended — only with specific, named evidence

myth.mythStatement: Your grandmother was right. The science now explains why. You do not have to choose between wisdom and evidence — Little Rituals is both.
myth.mythTest: Does this content honour the ritual as much as the product? Does it treat the parent as informed and capable, not anxious and needing reassurance?

examples.text: Wood-pressed at below 40°C. Above that temperature, the tocopherols — the Vitamin E that makes almond oil actually work on skin — start to degrade. We press below it. That is the only difference between our oil and most of what is available. It is also the difference between the oil your grandmother used and the one in most bottles on the shelf today.
examples.reason: Specific mechanism. Connects to tradition without romanticising it. Treats the parent as someone who can understand "tocopherol" once it is explained.

examples.text: The massage takes as long as it takes. The oil should not be the limiting factor.
examples.reason: Ritual-first. Product implied, not pushed. Short. Specific to the actual experience of the practice.

examples.text: You are going to do the massage anyway. You learnt it from your mother, and she learnt it from hers. We just want to make sure the oil is worth the time you give it.
examples.reason: Generational framing. Peer relationship — we are not teaching them to massage, they already know. Positions the product in service of the practice.

examples.text: Most baby skincare is designed for a baby in London or Los Angeles. Indian babies live in India — in its heat, its humidity, its particular quality of summer light. They also get the oil massage that Indian babies have always had. We made something that knows all of this.
examples.reason: Specific cultural positioning without putting down international brands directly. "Knows all of this" — personalisation claim grounded in specificity.

examples.text: Our products are completely toxic-free and chemical-free! Protect your baby from harmful ingredients! 🌿
examples.reason: Fear-based. Scientifically illiterate ("chemical-free"). Emoji in a context that requires substance. Screaming where calm confidence was needed.

examples.text: Give your baby the gift of nature's purest ingredients, inspired by ancient Indian wisdom. 🍃✨
examples.reason: Vague. "Nature's purest" is meaningless. "Ancient wisdom" without specificity is heritage-as-aesthetic. Emoji undermine the cultural grounding.

examples.text: You have already done the research. The gift is just how you share what you found.
examples.reason: Positions the giver as informed. The research is the value. Short. Warm.
